chapters.title: Chapter 4: Convexity: Where Duration Falls Short

lessons.title: Barbell vs Bullet: Using Convexity to Shape a Bond Portfolio

children.text: Here is a question that sounds impossible: can two bond portfolios have exactly the same duration, exactly the same rate risk by every measure in Chapter 3, and still behave differently when yields move? They can, and the difference is convexity. This is where convexity stops being a correction term in a formula and becomes something you can deliberately buy or sell when building a portfolio. Fund managers at every Indian AMC make this choice every month. This lesson shows you how, and what it costs.

body.text: Spread the same money across very short and very long bonds instead of concentrating it in the middle, and you keep the same duration but gain convexity. The market charges you for that in yield, so convexity is something you buy, not something you find.

markDefs.definition: A portfolio concentrated in bonds of a single maturity, clustered around the target duration.
A portfolio split between very short and very long bonds, with little or nothing in between, chosen so the weighted duration still hits the target.

children.text: portfolio puts everything at one point on the yield curve. A

puts weight at both ends and nothing in the middle, like the discs on a gym barbell. Build both to the same duration and their behaviour still differs, because convexity is a weighted average too, and it rises far faster with maturity than duration does.

body.latex: D_{\text{Portfolio}} = \sum_i w_i D_i \qquad\text{and}\qquad C_{\text{Portfolio}} = \sum_i w_i C_i
body.caption: Both duration and convexity are market-value-weighted averages. Matching duration says nothing about convexity, which is exactly the opening this lesson exploits.

children.text: Take three illustrative G-Secs on a normal upward-sloping curve, each priced at par at its own yield.

body.caption: The building blocks (illustrative G-Secs priced at par)

children.text: Look at the jump in convexity: from the 2-year to the 30-year, duration rises about six and a half times but convexity rises more than fifty times. That gap is what a barbell harvests. To match the bullet's duration of 7.09 using only the 2-year and 30-year bonds, solve for the weight w that makes w × 1.85 + (1 − w) × 12.11 = 7.09, which gives 48.9% in the 2-year and 51.1% in the 30-year.

body.title: Build a barbell to a target duration
body.prompt: You want a portfolio with a modified duration of 6.00, using only a 2-year bond with a modified duration of 1.85 and a 30-year bond with a modified duration of 12.47. What percentage should go into the 2-year bond? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: Solve w × 1.85 + (1 − w) × 12.47 = 6.00. Rearranged: w = (12.47 − 6.00) ÷ (12.47 − 1.85) = 6.47 ÷ 10.62 = 0.609, so 60.9% in the 2-year bond and 39.1% in the 30-year. Note how little of the long bond is needed: its duration does most of the work.

children.text: What the Extra Convexity Buys You
Now shift the whole curve up and down by the same amount and reprice both portfolios. Remember, they have identical duration, so duration alone predicts identical results.

body.caption: Price return for a parallel shift in yields: bullet vs barbell, same 7.09 duration

body.title: Same Duration, Different Payoff: Bullet vs Barbell (% price return)

children.text: The barbell wins in every row, up and down. That is what higher convexity means: more gain in a rally, less pain in a sell-off, for the same duration. But look at the size of the win. At ±25 basis points it is 0.02%, invisible next to the 9 basis points of yield you gave up. Only when yields move 100 basis points or more does the convexity advantage start to pay for itself.

body.label: The convexity trade in one line
body.value: Pay 9 bps a year, win 0.27% on a 100 bp move
body.context: Worth it if you expect a large move in either direction. A losing trade if yields sit still.

body.title: When does the barbell win?
body.question: Two portfolios have identical modified duration. The barbell has convexity of 124.5 and yields 9 basis points less than the bullet, whose convexity is 64.1. In which scenario does the bullet do better over one year?
options: Yields fall sharply by 200 basis points
Yields rise sharply by 200 basis points
Yields stay roughly where they are all year
The bullet can never do better, because the barbell has higher convexity
body.explanation: Convexity only pays when yields actually move. In a quiet year the barbell's higher convexity earns nothing, and its 9 basis points of extra yield income each year goes to the bullet. Convexity is not free: you pay for it in yield, so a flat market is when you regret buying it.

children.text: The Risk Duration Cannot See: Curve Twists

markDefs.definition: A change in the shape of the yield curve, where short and long yields move by different amounts, rather than every yield moving together.

children.text: Every number above assumes a parallel shift. Real yield curves rarely oblige. When RBI cuts rates, short yields usually fall more than long ones, and a curve can steepen or flatten without the 10-year moving at all. A
is precisely where a barbell and a bullet stop being interchangeable, and the effect is much larger than the convexity edge.

body.caption: Curve twists with the 10-year yield unchanged

body.text: Compare the numbers. A modest 25 basis point steepening costs the barbell 1.28%, nearly five times the 0.27% it gains from convexity on a 100 basis point parallel move. A barbell is not simply a better bullet: it is a bet that the curve will flatten, or at least not steepen much, wrapped around a convexity trade. Anyone selling you a barbell on convexity alone is showing you half the position.

columns.label: Bullet
points: Everything at one maturity, matched to the target duration
Lower convexity, so less benefit from large moves either way
Higher yield on a normal upward-sloping curve
Gains if the curve steepens; simplest to build and hold
Natural fit for a single goal on a known date

columns.label: Barbell
points: Split between very short and very long bonds
Higher convexity, so it beats the bullet on any large parallel move
Gives up yield, roughly 9 bps a year in our example
Gains if the curve flattens, loses if it steepens
Short leg matures regularly, giving cash to redeploy

body.title: What a barbell buys
body.textWithBlank: Compared with a bullet portfolio of the same duration, a barbell has higher ___, which is why it outperforms on large yield moves in either direction.
body.explanation: Convexity rises much faster with maturity than duration does, so combining very short and very long bonds gives more convexity than a single mid-maturity bond with the same duration.

body.title: A third shape: the ladder, and what Indian funds actually do

children.text: A ladder spreads money evenly across many maturities, say 1 through 10 years, with something maturing every year. Its convexity sits between a bullet and a barbell, and it has two practical advantages for individuals: regular cash flow as each rung matures, and no need to predict the curve. Many retail investors build ladders on RBI Retail Direct without ever using the word.

Among Indian debt funds, target maturity funds and roll-down funds are effectively bullets: they hold bonds maturing around a fixed date, and their duration shortens steadily as that date approaches. Dynamic bond funds move between shapes as the manager's view changes. Gilt funds and long duration funds often sit closer to a barbell, holding both liquid short-dated paper and long benchmark G-Secs. The factsheet's average maturity and Macaulay duration from Chapter 3 will not tell these shapes apart; for that you need the holdings list, which every AMC publishes monthly.

body.title: Rohini shapes a ₹2 crore bond allocation
body.scenario: Rohini Deshmukh runs a family office in Pune with ₹2 crore to place in G-Secs. Her view: inflation data has been volatile, the Union Budget is two months away, and she believes yields could move sharply, but she genuinely does not know in which direction. Her analyst proposes two options with identical duration of 7.09: a bullet of ₹2 crore in the 10-year G-Sec at 7.05%, or a barbell of ₹97.8 lakh in the 2-year at 6.60% and ₹1.02 crore in the 30-year at 7.30%, yielding 6.96% overall.
body.prompt: Explain what the barbell gains and costs in rupees under different outcomes, identify the risk that is not about convexity at all, and recommend a course of action.
body.modelAnswer:
1. Cost of the barbell: 9 basis points of yield on ₹2 crore, about ₹18,400 a year in lost income.
2. Gain if yields move sharply, from the parallel-shift table: at ±100 bps the barbell earns about 0.27% more, roughly ₹54,000. At ±200 bps it is about 0.94%, roughly ₹1.88 lakh. At ±300 bps, roughly ₹3.8 lakh. Note this holds whether yields rise or fall, which fits her view that the size of the move is more predictable than its direction.
3. Gain if yields barely move: nothing. She has simply paid ₹18,400 for insurance she did not use.
4. The risk that is not convexity: curve shape. If the curve steepens by just 25 basis points at each end, with the 10-year unchanged, the barbell loses about 1.28%, roughly ₹2.56 lakh, while the bullet is flat. That single risk is several times larger than the convexity edge she is buying. Post-Budget steepening is a real possibility when borrowing plans surprise the market.
5. Recommendation: the barbell is a reasonable expression of a big-move view, but she should hold it knowingly as a flattening bet as well, size it so a 25 to 50 basis point steepening is tolerable, and check the liquidity of the 30-year leg before committing ₹1 crore to it. If she has no view on curve shape at all, the bullet or a simple ladder is the more honest position.
6. Whichever she picks, she should recheck duration and weights after any large move, since the barbell's weights drift as the two legs move differently.

points: Duration and convexity are both weighted averages, so two portfolios can match on duration and differ sharply on convexity.
A barbell of 48.9% in a 2-year and 51.1% in a 30-year G-Sec matches a 10-year bullet's 7.09 duration but has convexity of 124.5 against 64.1.
Higher convexity means the barbell beats the bullet on any large parallel move, up or down: by 0.27% at 100 bps and 1.88% at 300 bps.
The market charges for convexity. Here it costs 9 basis points of yield a year, about ₹18,400 on ₹2 crore.
Convexity pays only if yields actually move. In a flat year, the bullet's higher yield wins.
A barbell is also a curve bet: a 25 bp steepening costs it 1.28%, several times its convexity advantage.
A ladder sits between the two and needs no view on the curve, which suits most individual investors.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Portfolios, bonds, yields and investors are illustrative, and all returns are price returns from immediate yield changes, before coupon income, costs and tax. Long-dated G-Secs can be less liquid for retail investors, and actual outcomes depend on how the whole yield curve moves. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before investing.
